title: Optical measurement is almost quantum: Quantum inspired universal optical bounds
abstract: Inspired by results in quantum information, we report the development of a formalism for optical sensing which abstracts the details of specific optical systems and allows us to form general bounds on measurement based only on the quantity to be measured. We find a universal bound that controls the performance of any passive optical system regardless of the technology used to construct it and that this bound is attained by a unique measurement scheme for each quantity of interest. Shockingly, our optical formalism is nearly identical to the quantum formalism, with essentially the same notions of the state to be measured and the operation of the measurement, along with an accompanying uncertainty principle.
summary: This work establishes a universal theoretical framework for bounding the precision of any passive optical measurement, generalizing concepts from quantum information theory. By deriving an optical Cramér-Rao bound, the authors show that the resulting formalism closely mirrors quantum mechanics, providing powerful, technology-agnostic limits for sensing applications. This is significant for understanding the fundamental limits of optical measurement beyond purely quantum regimes.
main_problem: The paper develops a general formalism to establish universal bounds on the performance of optical sensing, independent of the specific optical hardware used.
main_result: The derived optical measurement formalism is nearly identical to the quantum one, yielding a universal uncertainty principle that controls measurement performance for any passive optical system.
method: The authors adapt the quantum Cramér-Rao bound methodology, deriving a classical Fisher information for the optical case using a Pixel Operator Measure (POM) formalism.
model_or_system: The analysis applies to general passive optical systems, including imagers and interferometers, modeling the measurement as an expectation value derived from the electric field at the focal plane.

main_assumptions: The analysis assumes paraxial fields, a simple canonical detector response, and that electronics noise is the dominant source, independent of the field state.

paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the general formalism and the POM measurement description, derives the optical Cramér-Rao bound, and then applies this bound to specific sensing problems like wavefront aberration and depth estimation, comparing results to the quantum limit.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, generalized framework for quantum-inspired sensing limits in classical optics, showing deep structural parallels between classical measurement theory and quantum information theory.
